newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn ag official, traders differ on EU farm line.
newsitem.headline: Bonn ag official, traders differ on EU farm line.

text.p: Germany's agriculture ministry wishes to preserve the price-stabilising elements of the European Union farm policy which the trade believes may harm German food export goals, a country merchants seminar heard.

Franz-Josef Feiter, state secretary in the Bonn farm ministry, told a meeting at private agricultural school Burg Warberg, "EU farm policy is working and any existing uncertainty about compensation payments to farmers does not justify abandoning its vital elements."
"There is no alternative to securing farmers' incomes via transfer payments and acreage set-aside and this system should be defended in future world trade rounds," he said.
The EU Commission will release a set of recommendations for farm policy reform in mid-July and is likely to call for a greater decoupling of market and income policies.

Rudolf Stoehr, economist at grain trader Alfred C Toepfer, said German farmers should be encouraged to move away from their traditional reliance on support payments granted under the 1992 EU farm reform.
Rather than turning to support mechanisms such as grain intervention, which provides a safety net for prices, they should cut costs to be able to compete in expanding world food markets.
They should experiment with products outside those protected by intervention schemes and they should invest in finished food products, for example dairy and meat.
There was more than sufficient demand for such products in the former east bloc, North Africa, Asia and the Middle East.
This would earn farmers better margins and encourage a better grain market equilibrium to favour those farmers able to produce nearer the world market price.
Stoehr said a change of strategy was especially necessary for the time that central and eastern European countries (CEECs) joined the EU.

Future policy might include incentives for these countries to produce more raw materials such as grain and sugar beet in order to afford more sophisticated food products from the existing EU in return, he said.
Feiter said the CEECs needed long transition periods to bring the performance of their farm sectors in line with the EU.
The EU should acknowledge it could not yet produce at world market prices and plans to revolutionise current production patterns would not win support among the member countries.
Abandoning grain and oilseeds production would result in undesirable surplus production of dairy and meat products.
